tagline.text: A contemporary art museum in Antipolo with whitewashed Mediterranean-style buildings and gardens

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: November–May dry season (mornings recommended, as midday is hot)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,000 (admission, transport and a meal, per person)

children.text: The Pinto Art Museum is a contemporary art museum on a hill in Antipolo, with six white buildings and gardens spread over about twelve thousand square meters. It opened in 2010 and shows both contemporary and indigenous art, making it a popular day trip from Manila.

The Pinto Art Museum is a private museum in the Grand Heights subdivision of Antipolo, Rizal, east of Manila. Joven Cuanang, a collector who trained as a doctor, opened the Pinto Gallery around 2000 and developed it into the present museum in 2010. It is run by the Silangan Foundation for the Arts, Culture, and Ecology, which he co-founded. Six buildings stand on about
, and the grounds hold a contemporary art museum, an indigenous art museum, an art academy, a café and an arboretum of about

. Cuanang also co-founded the Antipolo Foundation for Arts, Culture, and Ecology after the 1986 People Power Revolution, and the museum is often presented as a case where one person's passion grew into a local artists' community.

The buildings were designed by Tony Leaño, a member of the Antipolo artists' group Saling Pusa. The style is organic and eclectic, mixing the bahay na bato (traditional Filipino stone house), Spanish colonial, American pueblo, mission, Greek and Balearic house styles. White walls, rounded arches, stone paths and stairs, ponds and tropical plants flow together so that buildings and gardens feel like one piece. The buildings are not air-conditioned and rely on open-air ventilation to preserve the collection, so midday can be hot.

The exhibitions center on Cuanang's collection and works by Saling Pusa members, covering contemporary and indigenous art. Gallery 7, which opened in January 2020, is the largest contemporary exhibition space. Exhibits change often, so you can see different works on each visit, and some are interactive installations. In the 1990s Cuanang was also known for "Sampayan Art," exhibiting local artists' works on a clothesline. Guides say a stamped ticket allows same-day re-entry, so you can go for lunch and come back to see buildings you missed.

The museum's roots lie in Saling Pusa, a group of local Antipolo artists. Cuanang supported this group of amateur artists, the works accumulated, and the collection grew into a formal museum. As a result, the exhibits have a strong local, hand-made feel unlike large Manila museums, and the buildings themselves look like works of imagination. The story of selling local works hung on a clothesline in the 1990s is often told as an amusing scene in Philippine modern art history. This guide is for travelers who want to spend a day pairing the museum with Antipolo Cathedral or Hinulugang Taktak, and for people looking for photogenic places. It sorts out the admission fees, rules and directions that can be confusing. For visitors from abroad, it offers a quiet place to walk and take photos away from the shopping malls and churches of central Manila. The phone number is listed as (02) 8697-1015 and the email as pintoartmuseum@yahoo.com, but fees and opening hours change often, so check the latest information on official channels.

Galleries 1 to 7 are linked by gardens and stone paths, so walking between the buildings is part of the visit. Winding paths, arches and sculptures make almost every corner photogenic. The paths twist, so walk slowly and check where the works are on the map. Each building has different ceiling heights and window shapes, so even the same white walls feel different as light comes in. The view of Antipolo's hills and the city through the arches is also a popular photo spot.

The galleries show paintings, sculpture and installations by Filipino artists. Guide materials mention artists such as Elmer Borlongan, Rodel Tapaya, Mark Justiniani and BenCab. Some exhibits are said to have QR codes linking to artist statements. Exhibits differ from one period to the next, so check locally.

A separate building presents crafts and carvings of the Philippines' indigenous peoples. Seen alongside the contemporary art, it lets you compare how today's artists draw inspiration from tradition. There is no set order, so start with whichever building appeals to you. The indigenous art collection is described as one the founder gathered over many years, so read the exhibit labels slowly.

Opened in January 2020, this is the largest contemporary exhibition space. Its high ceilings and broad walls suit large works and installation art. Parts of it may be closed while exhibits are changed, so check before you go.
The arboretum covers about

and held about 500 indigenous plant species as of 2021. Ponds and shade trees between the buildings make good places to rest after viewing the art. Paths get slippery in the rainy season, so watch your footwear.
The on-site café, Café Rizal by Peppermill, is described as serving meals with garden views. A main dish costs about
, and last orders are listed at around
. Outside food cannot be brought in.

A school called the Pinto Academy teaches literature, visual arts and performing arts. The museum is used not only for exhibitions but also as a gathering place for local artists and students. Event and performance schedules vary, so check the official channels. Timing your visit to a particular event can give you a livelier atmosphere.
Leave Manila and head to Antipolo by Grab, taxi or jeepney.
Enter at opening time and look around the gardens and Galleries 1–3 while it is quiet.
See Gallery 7 and the indigenous art museum, then rest on a bench by the ponds.
Have lunch at Café Rizal.
Go to Antipolo Cathedral and look around the church and the plaza stalls.
Weekend roads at the entrance are crowded, so arriving right at opening is easier. Moving through the museum takes time, so allow 20–30 minutes per building rather than rushing between galleries.
Spend the morning at the Pinto Art Museum.
Have lunch in town and visit Antipolo Cathedral.
Take a walk in Hinulugang Taktak park.

Take a jeepney or FX from Cubao or Pasig to Antipolo and get off near Antipolo Cathedral, Ynares Center or Robinsons Antipolo. From there, tell a tricycle driver "Grand Heights" and it will take you to the museum entrance.
From Manila to Antipolo it takes
1–2 hours
depending on traffic.

Take Ortigas Avenue Extension past Tikling Junction and turn right at Unciano Medical Center to reach the Grand Heights subdivision. You can also take Marcos Highway through Marikina to Sumulong Highway.
Search "Pinto Art Museum" on Google Maps or Waze. Parking is listed as free, but it is customary to tip the parking attendants.
You can also ride LRT-2 to Antipolo Station and transfer to a jeepney or Grab. From the station to the museum takes about
20–40 minutes
depending on traffic.
After buying a ticket at the entrance, you walk between the buildings. The terrain is hilly, with many steps and slopes.
With no air conditioning and many gardens, the dry season is best. Of the day, the hours right after opening are quiet and the light is soft.

From around 3 p.m. until closing, warm light falls on the outdoor gardens, which is good for photos. Weekends and holidays are busy, so weekdays are recommended. During exhibit changes or events some buildings may be closed, so check the official channels before you go.

You can visit in the rainy season too, but when showers come, the outdoor stone paths and steps get slippery and you should slow down. In that season, do the indoor galleries first and see the gardens once the rain stops.

Antipolo is an easy day trip from Manila, so most travelers stay in Manila or Quezon City. Hotel names and rates vary by season, so check recent reviews on booking sites.

The most convenient place to eat is the on-site Café Rizal. Dishes mentioned include sinigang na baboy (sour pork soup), beef tapa and truffle pasta. In Antipolo town there are many Filipino restaurants and fast-food outlets, and stalls in front of the cathedral sell roasted cashews and kalamay.

When planning, arrive at opening time, see the indoor galleries in the morning, and take in the gardens and ponds after lunch. Combining it with Antipolo Cathedral or Hinulugang Taktak on the same day keeps travel short, and having dinner back in Manila is safer. Café orders close shortly before the museum does, so eat lunch early.
Tickets are listed as sold on-site only, and cash is convenient. A stamped ticket is said to allow same-day re-entry.
Closing time is listed as either 5 p.m. or 6 p.m., depending on the source. Check before you go.
The museum is listed as closed on Mondays.
Tripods, flash and video recording are listed as prohibited inside the galleries, so follow the rules.
Do not touch the artworks or outdoor installations.
Large bags may be inspected, and outside food and drinks cannot be brought in.
You need comfortable shoes, a hat and water, and an umbrella in the rainy season.
Professional shoots are said to need prior approval and may incur fees.
There is a ramp at the main entrance, but the hilly terrain makes some areas hard to reach by wheelchair.
There is no playground, so keep an eye on children.
The buildings are not air-conditioned and many paths slope, so watch for heat and dehydration at midday.
Stone paths and steps make some areas hard to navigate with wheelchairs and strollers.
Weekend roads at the entrance are jammed, so arrive right at opening.
Touching the artworks and outdoor installations is listed as prohibited, so enjoy them with your eyes only.
Fees and opening hours can change, so check the official channels for the latest announcements.
If you come by public transport, tell the tricycle driver "Grand Heights."
